presentingComplaint: 2 days of frequent bloody, mucoid stools with painful straining and fever
history: Previously well 34-year-old man presenting with a 2-day history of frequent small-volume bloody diarrhoea (10-12 stools/day) mixed with mucus, associated with lower abdominal cramping, painful ineffectual straining at stool, and fever with chills. Symptoms began ~24h after eating at a roadside eatery; two household contacts have milder loose stools. No recent travel abroad, no antibiotics in the preceding 90 days, no prior hospitalisation. No known immunosuppression. Mild reduced oral intake with thirst.
examination: Alert but uncomfortable and mildly dehydrated (dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor). Abdomen soft with lower-abdominal and left-iliac-fossa tenderness, no guarding or rigidity, active bowel sounds; no palpable masses. Rectal exam shows blood-and-mucus streaking. Pertinent negatives: no jaundice, no hepatosplenomegaly, no rash, no neck stiffness, no peritonism.

labs.WBC: 14.2 x10^9/L with neutrophilia and left shift
labs.Stool microscopy: numerous RBCs and sheets of pus cells (fecal leukocytes)

imaging: Not indicated in uncomplicated invasive diarrhoea; abdominal films reserved for suspected toxic megacolon or perforation, neither present here
microbiology: Stool culture sent (Shigella/Salmonella/Campylobacter); stool for ova/cysts to exclude amoebiasis. Blood cultures obtained given fever. Results pending; empirical management started on clinical grounds.
finalDiagnosis: Dysentery (invasive bacterial diarrhea, most likely Shigella)
citations: Harrison 22e — Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning / Shigellosis
IDSA Infectious Diarrhea Diagnosis and Management 2017
stewardship: Empiric ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone) is guideline-concordant first-line for febrile invasive bacterial dysentery pending cultures; azithromycin is preferred where fluoroquinolone resistance is prevalent (e.g., many South/Southeast Asian Shigella/Campylobacter isolates). Oral/IV rehydration is the cornerstone of care. De-escalate/stop per stool culture and susceptibilities; avoid antimotility agents.
contraindications: Avoid loperamide/antimotility agents in bloody diarrhoea (risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged shedding, esp. Shiga-toxin E. coli)
Fluoroquinolone: caution with QT prolongation, tendinopathy, and known local resistance
Avoid empiric antibiotics if STEC/EHEC suspected (raises HUS risk); reassess if hemolysis/AKI emerge
edgeCases: Amoebic colitis can mimic bacterial dysentery but classically has fewer fecal leukocytes and requires antiparasitic (metronidazole + luminal agent), not fluoroquinolone
Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli presents with bloody diarrhoea but antibiotics may precipitate HUS
Progression to toxic megacolon or intestinal perforation warrants urgent surgical/imaging evaluation
expectedMaiK: Classic febrile invasive bacterial dysentery with bloody, mucoid, small-volume stools, tenesmus and fecal leukocytes points to Shigella-type colitis; prioritise rehydration and a stool culture, give empiric ciprofloxacin (or azithromycin where fluoroquinolone resistance is high), and explicitly avoid antimotility drugs. Keep amoebic colitis and STEC on the differential.
expectedNextQuestions: Any recent travel, sick contacts, or common-source food exposure?
Is there tenesmus and true blood/mucus in the stool versus watery diarrhoea?
Any features suggesting HUS or complications (reduced urine output, pallor, worsening pain/distension)?
expectedInvestigations: Stool microscopy for fecal leukocytes, RBCs, and ova/cysts (amoeba)
CBC, CRP, electrolytes and renal function

investigations: Stool microscopy for fecal leukocytes and ova/cysts

regressionAssertions: stewardship must recommend empiric fluoroquinolone or azithromycin, not an antimotility agent
